standard.title: Resources, needs and wants
standard.description: types of resources, including natural, human and capital, and how they satisfy needs and wants
standard.prior_knowledge: Foundation–Year 4 HASS concepts: Students have prior understanding of communities, places, and basic ideas about goods and services. Year 4 content introduces government and services, providing indirect context for economic concepts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the types of resources — natural, human and capital — and how they are used in production to satisfy the needs and wants of communities, including consideration of sustainable resource use.

nodes.label: Needs and wants
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between needs (essential for survival and wellbeing) and wants (desirable but not essential), and give examples of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Define 'needs' and 'wants', give two examples of each, and explain the difference.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the distinction between needs (food, water, shelter, safety) and wants (entertainment, luxury goods, non-essential services), and discuss that the boundary between needs and wants can vary by context, culture and community.
wider: Explore how needs and wants differ between communities in high-income and low-income countries, and evaluate whether all needs are currently being met globally
Investigate how advertising shapes people's perceptions of what they 'need', and discuss the distinction between manufactured wants and genuine needs
nodes.hinge_reason: The needs/wants distinction is conceptually foundational for understanding scarcity, resource allocation, and the purpose of production. Students who conflate the two will not understand why resources must be allocated or why sustainability is necessary.

response_modes.reason: Use a sorting activity with concrete items to establish the distinction, including some genuinely ambiguous cases (e.g. is a phone a need or a want in contemporary life?) to build nuanced understanding rather than a rigid binary.

success_criteria: Students define 'needs' and 'wants' and give two examples of each.
Students explain why the distinction between needs and wants matters for thinking about resource use.

nodes.label: Types of resources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can categorise resources as natural, human or capital, give examples of each type, and explain how each type contributes to the production of goods and services.
nodes.minimum_width: Name and define three types of resources (natural, human, capital) and give one example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Categorise resources as natural (water, coal, wheat), human (workers, business owners, volunteers, managers) and capital (tools, machines, technologies), and explain how each type is used in the production of goods and services that satisfy needs and wants.
wider: Investigate the factors of production used in a specific local industry (e.g. farming, manufacturing, services) and explain how natural, human and capital resources combine to produce goods or services
Explore how technology is changing the role of human resources in production, and discuss what this means for workers and communities

response_modes.reason: The three-category resource classification is a prerequisite vocabulary for economic analysis — students need fluency with the categories and examples before they can analyse production or evaluate sustainability.

success_criteria: Students correctly categorise at least two examples of each resource type.
Students explain how each type of resource contributes to producing a named good or service.

nodes.label: How resources satisfy needs and wants
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how natural, human and capital resources are combined in production to satisfy the needs and wants of communities.
nodes.minimum_width: Trace how resources (natural, human, capital) are combined to produce one good or service and explain which need or want it satisfies.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how the three types of resources are combined in the production of goods and services for a local community, identifying the factors of production used and the needs or wants satisfied by several different examples.
wider: Map the full supply chain for a common consumer product and identify all three resource types at each stage of production
Compare resource use in subsistence economies with market economies, and discuss how each system satisfies community needs and wants

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from tracing the resource-to-satisfaction pathway across multiple different goods and services — this builds transferable economic reasoning rather than a single worked example.

success_criteria: Students trace the three resource types used in producing at least one good or service.
Students explain which need or want the production satisfies.

nodes.label: Sustainable resource use
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why sustainable resource use is important, and describe how resources might be used more sustainably to meet current and future needs and wants.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what 'sustainable resource use' means and give one example of a more sustainable practice.
nodes.typical_width: Explain why sustainable resource use is important — that resources are finite and that current use patterns affect future availability — and describe strategies for using resources more sustainably, with examples from natural, human and capital resource categories.
wider: Investigate a specific resource management challenge (e.g. water scarcity, soil degradation, energy transition) and evaluate proposed solutions for sustainability

Explore how First Nations Australian resource management practices (e.g. seasonal harvesting, firestick farming) model sustainable use, and consider what modern economies can learn from these approaches

response_modes.reason: Sustainable resource use integrates the needs/wants distinction (Node 1), the resource types (Node 2), and the production process (Node 3). Students need to connect all three to make a reasoned sustainability judgment.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations resource management practices as a model for sustainable use is a pedagogically rich and culturally significant direction — it connects economic concepts to genuine environmental and cultural knowledge with contemporary relevance.
success_criteria: Students explain what sustainable resource use means and why it matters.
Students describe at least one strategy for using resources more sustainably.
Students connect sustainable resource use to meeting both current and future needs and wants.
